key_terms.meaning: p(λ) = det(λI − A), a monic polynomial of degree n whose roots are the eigenvalues; det(A − λI) gives the same roots.
A scalar λ such that det(A − λI) = 0, that is, A − λI is singular.
A nonzero vector x with Ax = λx; it lies in the null space of A − λI.
The number of times λ appears as a root of the characteristic polynomial.
The dimension of the null space of A − λI, i.e. the number of independent eigenvectors for that λ.
tr(A) = sum of the diagonal entries = sum of all eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity.
A* = A (conjugate transpose equals A); all eigenvalues are real.
U*U = I; every eigenvalue has modulus 1 and the matrix is unitarily diagonalizable.
QᵀQ = I; eigenvalues satisfy |λ| = 1 and Q⁻¹ = Qᵀ.
Aᵀ = −A; eigenvalues are purely imaginary or zero.
AA* = A*A; such a matrix is always unitarily diagonalizable, so it has n independent eigenvectors.
The matrix obtained by putting A into a polynomial p; its eigenvalues are p(λᵢ) for each eigenvalue λᵢ of A.
Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial: p(A) = 0.
The monic polynomial m of lowest degree with m(A) = 0; it divides every polynomial that kills A.
A matrix A with A = PDP⁻¹, where D is diagonal and P is invertible; possible exactly when there are n independent eigenvectors.
A = QDQᵀ with Q orthogonal and D diagonal; possible exactly when A is real symmetric.
A function q(x) = xᵀAx with A taken symmetric; in two variables it is ax² + 2hxy + by².
The sum of squares c₁y₁² + c₂y₂² + … + cₙyₙ² obtained after a change of variables y = P⁻¹x.
For a canonical form with p positive and q negative squares, the index is q and the signature is p − q (some books write the pair (p, q)).
Positive definite if q(x) > 0 for all x ≠ 0, negative definite if q(x) < 0, indefinite if it takes both signs.

takeaways: Eigenvalues are the roots of det(λI − A) = 0, and the eigenvectors for a given λ are the nonzero vectors in the null space of A − λI.
The trace gives the sum of the eigenvalues and the determinant gives their product, both counted with algebraic multiplicity.
For each eigenvalue, 1 ≤ geometric multiplicity ≤ algebraic multiplicity; equality for all eigenvalues is exactly the condition for diagonalizability.
The Cayley–Hamilton theorem turns the characteristic polynomial into a matrix identity p(A) = 0, which gives fast ways to compute A⁻¹ and high powers of A.
A is diagonalizable exactly when it has n linearly independent eigenvectors, which then form the columns of the diagonalizing matrix P.
A real symmetric matrix always has real eigenvalues and a full set of mutually orthogonal eigenvectors, so it can be diagonalized by an orthogonal matrix.
A quadratic form with matrix A becomes a sum of squares under a change of variables; an orthogonal change uses the eigenvalues as the coefficients.
Rank, index and signature of a quadratic form do not depend on which reduction you choose, so they classify the form and the conic it represents.
bank_note: Long answers here are mostly full computations — find the characteristic polynomial, the eigenvalues with multiplicities, the diagonalizing or orthonormalizing matrix, then reduce the quadratic form and read off rank, index, signature and nature — with the supporting theorem stated cleanly before it is used.

bank.q: Define eigenvalue and eigenvector of a square matrix A. Write the characteristic equation for a 2 × 2 matrix and use it to find the eigenvalues and one eigenvector for each eigenvalue of A = [[2, 1], [1, 3]].
outline: Ax = λx with x ≠ 0
det(A − λI) = 0, i.e. λ² − (tr A)λ + det A = 0
eigenvalues 1 and 4 for this matrix
solve (A − λI)x = 0 for each λ and pick a nonzero solution

bank.q: State the rules relating eigenvalues of A to the trace, the determinant, the powers Aᵏ, the inverse A⁻¹ and a polynomial p(A). Explain why each rule holds.
outline: sum of eigenvalues = tr(A) from the coefficient of λⁿ⁻¹
product of eigenvalues = det(A) from the constant term
eigenvalues of Aᵏ are λᵢᵏ with the same eigenvectors
eigenvalues of A⁻¹ are 1/λᵢ when A is nonsingular
eigenvalues of p(A) are p(λᵢ)

bank.q: State the Cayley–Hamilton theorem. Use it to find A⁻¹ and A⁴ for A = [[1, 2], [2, 1]] without computing eigenvectors.
outline: statement p(A) = 0 for p(λ) = det(λI − A)
here p(λ) = λ² − 2λ − 3
A² − 2A − 3I = 0
multiply by A⁻¹ to get A⁻¹ = (A − 2I)/3
reduce A³ and A⁴ using A² = 2A + 3I

bank.q: Define algebraic and geometric multiplicity of an eigenvalue. State the necessary and sufficient condition for a matrix to be diagonalizable, and prove that distinct eigenvalues always give independent eigenvectors.
outline: definitions of both multiplicities
1 ≤ GM ≤ AM for every eigenvalue
A diagonalizable iff GM = AM for all eigenvalues iff there are n independent eigenvectors
independence proof by applying (A − λᵢI) repeatedly

bank.q: Define a quadratic form in n variables and the symmetric matrix of a quadratic form. Write the matrix of q(x, y, z) = 3x² + 5y² − 2z² + 4xy − 6xz + 2yz and state its rank and definiteness.
outline: q(x) = xᵀAx with A symmetric
diagonal entries are the squared-term coefficients, off-diagonal halve the cross-term coefficients
A written out
rank from nonzero eigenvalues or reduction
definiteness from eigenvalue signs

bank.q: Diagonalize A = [[1, 0, 0], [1, 2, 0], [2, 1, 3]] by finding P and D with A = PDP⁻¹, and verify the result.
outline: characteristic polynomial (1 − λ)(2 − λ)(3 − λ)
eigenvalues 1, 2, 3, all simple so diagonalizable
eigenvectors solved from (A − λI)x = 0
P with the eigenvectors as columns, D the diagonal of eigenvalues
check AP = PD

bank.q: Orthogonally diagonalize A = [[2, 1, 1], [1, 2, 1], [1, 1, 2]]. Find an orthogonal Q and diagonal D with QᵀAQ = D.
outline: eigenvalues 4 (once) and 1 (twice), all real
eigenvector (1, 1, 1) for λ = 4
two independent eigenvectors for λ = 1, chosen orthogonal
normalise all three to get orthonormal columns of Q, D = diag(4, 1, 1)
verify QᵀQ = I and QᵀAQ = D

bank.q: Reduce the quadratic form q = 2x₁² + 2x₂² + 2x₃² − 2x₁x₂ − 2x₂x₃ − 2x₁x₃ to canonical form by an orthogonal transformation. State its rank, index, signature and nature.
outline: symmetric matrix A built from the coefficients
eigenvalues 0, 3, 3
orthonormal eigenvectors give x = Qy
canonical form 3y₂² + 3y₃²
rank 2, index 0, signature 2, positive semi-definite

bank.q: Reduce q = x² + 2y² + 3z² + 2xy − 2yz to canonical form by completing squares, and find the rank, index and signature.
outline: group all x-terms: (x + y)²
substitute X = x + y to clear the cross term
remaining terms in y, z reduced further
count positive and negative squares
rank = number of nonzero squares, index = number of negative ones, signature = p − q

bank.q: Using the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, find the inverse of A = [[1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 5], [3, 5, 6]] and express A⁵ as a linear combination of A², A and I.
outline: characteristic polynomial of degree 3 by expansion
p(A) = 0 written out
rearrange the constant term to get A⁻¹ as a polynomial in A
divide λ⁵ by p(λ) to get a remainder of degree 2
the same identity holds for A

bank.q: Find the nature of the conic 5x² + 4xy + 2y² − 6 = 0 by diagonalizing its quadratic part, and sketch the reduced form.
outline: eigenvalues 1 and 6, both positive
orthogonal change gives 6X² + Y² = 6, an ellipse
semi-axes from the constants
eigenvalue signs decide ellipse, hyperbola or parabola

bank.q: Prove that eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues of a matrix are linearly independent, and deduce that a matrix with n distinct eigenvalues is diagonalizable. Show by an example that repeated eigenvalues need not destroy diagonalizability.
outline: independence argument applying (A − λᵢI) to a dependence relation
n independent eigenvectors form a basis, so P is invertible
distinct eigenvalues give AM = GM = 1
counter-example such as identity or a repeated-eigenvalue matrix that is still diagonalizable
contrast with a defective example

bank.q: Prove that a real symmetric matrix has only real eigenvalues and that eigenvectors from different eigenvalues are orthogonal. State the spectral theorem and explain how it gives orthogonal diagonalization.
outline: real eigenvalue proof using x̄ᵀAx and symmetry
orthogonality proof using (Ax)ᵀy = xᵀ(Ay)
repeated eigenvalues handled by Gram–Schmidt inside the eigenspace
spectral theorem: A = QDQᵀ with Q orthogonal
consequence: full set of orthonormal eigenvectors

bank.q: A 3 × 3 matrix has characteristic polynomial (λ − 2)³ and minimal polynomial (λ − 2)². Discuss whether it is diagonalizable, and explain how the minimal polynomial decides this in general. Add a note on why index and signature of a quadratic form are independent of the reduction used.
outline: AM = 3 for λ = 2
minimal polynomial has a repeated factor so A is not diagonalizable
diagonalizable iff the minimal polynomial has distinct linear factors
GM equals the number of Jordan blocks for that eigenvalue
Sylvester's law of inertia: number of positive and negative squares is fixed
rank, index and signature therefore are invariants of the form

glossary.def: A scalar λ for which Ax = λx has a nonzero solution x.
A nonzero vector x that is mapped by A to a scalar multiple of itself.
The null space of A − λI, containing the zero vector and all eigenvectors for λ.
The equation det(A − λI) = 0 whose roots are the eigenvalues.
The polynomial det(λI − A) of degree n in λ.
The set of all eigenvalues of a matrix, with multiplicities.
How many times an eigenvalue repeats as a root of the characteristic polynomial.
The number of independent eigenvectors available for one eigenvalue.
A matrix whose geometric multiplicity is smaller than the algebraic multiplicity for some eigenvalue, so it is not diagonalizable.
Matrices A and B with B = P⁻¹AP for some invertible P; they share eigenvalues, trace, determinant and characteristic polynomial.
Similar to a diagonal matrix, that is, A = PDP⁻¹ with D diagonal.
A real square matrix Q with QᵀQ = I, whose columns form an orthonormal basis.
A complex square matrix U with U*U = I.
A complex square matrix equal to its own conjugate transpose.
A matrix that commutes with its conjugate transpose, AA* = A*A.
The statement that p(A) = 0 whenever p is the characteristic polynomial of A.
The lowest-degree monic polynomial m with m(A) = 0.
A homogeneous polynomial of degree two in several variables, written xᵀAx with A symmetric.
A sum of squared new variables obtained from a quadratic form by an invertible linear change of variables.
The number of nonzero squares in a canonical form, equal to the rank of its symmetric matrix.
The number of negative squares in a canonical form.
The difference p − q between the numbers of positive and negative squares.
q(x) > 0 for every nonzero x; all eigenvalues of the symmetric matrix are positive.
A quadratic form that takes both positive and negative values, so its eigenvalues have both signs.
The numbers of positive, negative and zero squares in a canonical form depend only on the matrix, not on the change of variables chosen.
